results.why: Names sync-payments rewriting paid_at on archived rows and states how the plan handles it. The migration task has a down step and a test that checks the down section. Every task names its files and starts with a failing test. Fails item 2: it labels the cleanup conflict 'decision needed' but builds the guard into Task 4 and says 'I chose to follow the spec'. Nothing invented beyond the spec.

Flags syncPayments re-settling archived invoices as a risk. Item 2 is only partial: it sets the guard as the default and asks for confirmation afterward. The migration has a down step but no test of it; it only suggests testing against a real database 'separately'. The steps don't name tests per task or put tests first; tests are batched into step 5. The index on archived_at is an implementation detail, not a new requirement.

The tasks are well structured: files listed, failing test first, and a migration test that checks the down section. Sync-payments is noted in Review Focus as accepted. It chooses the cleanup fix: recommends option (a) and Task 4 assumes it. It invents a scope limit of 4 files ('your limit is 4') and splits the work into two PRs on that basis, but its scope_threshold lookup came back empty. Its claims that plan-check was clean and that a reviewer approved aren't shown in the output it printed.

Asks the user directly about the cleanup conflict, lists the options, and holds the Task 4 change 'pending the answer'. Raises sync-payments as a second writer in an explicit open question. The migration has a down step plus an up-then-down test, with a fallback check that both sections exist. Steps aren't written as file-plus-failing-test-first tasks; tests come in a batch at the end.

Brings up sync-payments only for job ordering, never as a second writer that can change paid_at on archived invoices. Proposes a default cleanup fix and asks for confirmation, so item 2 is partial. The migration has a down step and a verify step that runs up then down on a scratch database. Tests come in a batch at the end, not first in each task.

Names syncPayments and markPaid as second writers of paid_at. Review Focus 2 and an open question cover them, with a default and a checklist line in Task 4. The migration task has a down step and a failing test of the up/down SQL first. Every task names its files and starts with a failing test and its run command. It invents no requirement, and the git-remote claim is backed by command output. It fails item 2: it decided the cleanup change itself (Task 3 adds the guard and the merge order depends on it), then only asked for confirmation.

Mentions that sync-payments rewrites paid_at, but leaves it out of scope rather than planning for it. It flags the cleanup conflict as the user's call, but step 4 already applies the proposed guard. The migration has a down step, but the up/down/up test is skipped when no DB is available. There are no per-task failing tests: the tests are lumped into step 5. It invents nothing.

Step 6 handles the sync-payments rewrite of archived rows. It frames the cleanup fix as needing sign-off but proposes one resolution and puts it into step 5. The down step exists, but the migration test is conditional on a runner existing. It has no test-first tasks. It invents an index on archived_at, which the spec does not ask for.

Review Focus 5 notes the sync-payments/markPaid rewrite, but only as a note. Task 4 already adds the cleanup guard and asks the user to confirm afterwards. Step 6 treats the re-payment rewrite as a decision with a default. The down step exists and an up/down test is listed, but separately from the migration task. It has no test-first tasks. It invents an index on archived_at.

Each task names its files and starts with a failing test. Re-settlement by sync-payments is a review focus and is pinned by a test. The migration test checks that a down section exists. Step 1 adds the now and send seams before the feature work. Step 4 plans the sent-record as dueSoonSentAt on the invoice, and every test uses a fake send. All reminder tests come after the change, so no test pins today's overdue behaviour first (AC 4). It also adds behaviour the spec never asks for: a per-invoice try/catch with logging and retry on failure. Every repo claim matches a file it read.

It does a behaviour-preserving refactor that injects send and now before the feature. It plans the AC3 record as an in-memory Set, notes that a restart clears it, and uses a fake send in tests. It raises dueAt format and overdue dedupe as questions instead of deciding them. The overdue test only appears in the test step after the feature, so AC 4 is not pinned before the change. Its repo claims match the files it read.

Task 1 injects the clock and mailer and writes overdue tests before the due-soon feature. Task 2 plans dueSoonSentAt. However, Task 1 Step 2 expects the test to fail because 'the real fetch is attempted'. That run would send to mail.internal, which breaks the no-real-email rule. It also invents rules for skipping missing or unparseable dueAt values, which the spec does not state.

It refactors in the now and send seams first, plans the dedupe flag on the invoice, and uses a fake send in every test. It raises the template name, restart behaviour and overdue repeats as open questions. Tests are written after the feature steps, so nothing pins today's overdue behaviour before the change. Its repo claims are grounded in the files it read.

Task 1 is a behaviour-preserving seam for now and send, with overdue characterization tests (including resend on every run) written before any feature task. A globalThis.fetch stub that throws means no test can reach the network. Task 3 plans dueSoonSentAt explicitly. Scope stays tight, and persistence and the meaning of 'days' are raised as questions. Its process claims are backed by output: plan-check printed exit 0, and a reviewer subagent was run. Retry on failed send is a small addition, but the plan marks it as review focus.

Task 1 writes characterization tests of the overdue path and runs them against unchanged code, with global fetch stubbed. Only then does it add the injectable now/send seams, and it does this before any feature task. AC3's dueSoonSentAt record is planned explicitly. The plan raises the UTC-day reading and the failure behaviour as decisions for the user, so it invents no requirement. plan-check passed and a review round was applied. One unsupported claim: 'no origin remote'. No command output shown checks the remotes.

Step 1 is a no-behaviour-change refactor that adds the { now, send } seams and a test pinning overdue, before any feature work. The dueSoonSentAt record is planned. Timezone, retry and scheduling are raised as open questions. Every test uses a fake send. It loses a point because the overdue test is added in the same step as the refactor rather than before it, and the plan has less executable detail (no per-task verify commands).

The seam refactor comes first and the dueSoonSentAt record is planned. Tests use a fake send, and the assumptions are flagged as decisions for the user. The plan was given only in the reply and was not written to a file.

The seam refactor comes first. The sent-record is planned as a Set exposed through hasSent/markSent, and the plan notes the restart limitation. Tests use a fake send. All tests come in step 5, after the feature changes, so overdue behaviour is not pinned before the change. Its claims match the code it read.

Task 1 adds the clock and mailer seam first, with overdue tests written before the change, and dueSoonSentAt is planned.
